title: Centralized Policy Orchestration: control-plane routing enforcement proposal
content:
Purpose:
This note proposes a single, pragmatic approach to policy orchestration for routing and control plane authorization across multi-region Redwood deployments. It focuses on where to enforce policies (enforcement points), how to express them (ABAC/RBAC hybrid), and runtime considerations for velocity, reliability, and observability. Goal is to converge on a small set of clear insertion points and a lightweight orchestration model so teams can reason about end-to-end guarantees without incurring big latency or operational overhead.

Context and problem statement:
- We operate a global control plane and region-local data planes (hosted, dedicated, private). Requests traverse multiple components: edge ingress, regional gateways/load-balancers, routing service, model-serving clusters, and administrative control APIs.
- Teams need different policy semantics: customer isolation, route-level quotas, SLO-differentiated routing, data residency checks, and feature flags controlling fallbacks.
- Current ad-hoc enforcement is spread across proxy filters, service code, and infra config (Nginx/LB rules, Envoy filters, runtime feature flags). This leads to:
  - Inconsistent semantics across regions
  - Hard-to-audit enforcement surface
  - Duplication and drift when policies change

Design principles:
1) Single source of truth for policy definitions (Policy Catalog) but multiple enforcement points that are clearly classified.
2) Keep request-path authorization as close to request routing decisions as possible (to avoid stale allow/deny decisions after routing has occurred).
3) Prefer fast, cacheable checks at the edge for coarse-grained policies; defer fine-grained checks to the regional control plane or model-serving node.
4) Support a hybrid ABAC (attribute-based) + RBAC model: RBAC for bounded administrative operations, ABAC for per-request decisions (customer data, model id, region).
5) All enforcement must produce audit events and sampling traces; observable failures should trigger safe fallback behavior.

High-level architecture:
- Policy Catalog (central control-plane service): stores policy definitions, versioning, tags (region, tenant, stage), and evaluation hints. Policies express conditions over attributes (tenant_id, route, model_variant, region, request_size, origin_ip, deployment_tier).
- Policy Distribution: incremental push via signed bundles + versioned delta to regional control planes; fallback to pull via signed storage (S3-like) for private deployments.
- Enforcement library / SDK: language-neutral small library (gRPC + local cache) used by routing service, gateway proxy plugins, and model-serving agents.
- Enforcement Points: standardized insertion points where the SDK is invoked and decisions are enforced.

Recommended enforcement points and rationale:
1) Edge ingress (pre-routing coarse checks)
   - What to enforce: IP allowlist/denylist, global rate-limits, simple tenant-level deny/soft-block, geo-residency check.
   - Why: fast rejection of obviously invalid traffic; reduces backend load.
   - Performance: must be cache-first, evaluated via fast match tables (Envoy RBAC-like).
   - Failure mode: if policy service unreachable, default to last-known-good bundle; configurable fail-open/fail-closed per tenant.

2) Routing service (policy-aware routing decisions)
   - What to enforce: route-level policies (preferred region, model_variant constraints, SLO tier), A/B rollout gate (canary token check), cross-tenant routing isolation.
   - Why: routing decisions must consider policy to pick correct backend (e.g., dedicated pool vs hosted).
   - Implementation: call enforcement SDK synchronously (sub-1ms cache hit target) or pre-warm decisions with local evaluation engine.

3) Regional control-plane gateway (post-routing, pre-invoke checks)
   - What to enforce: quota consumption, feature entitlements, data-handling flags (e.g., PII-scrub required), cryptographic attestations for private deployments.
   - Why: regional policies might supplement central policies (data residency, local compliance).
   - Note: this layer reconciles central policy versions with local overrides (policy precedence rules needed).

4) Model-serving agent / runtime (final authority for sensitive ops)
   - What to enforce: model-level access restrictions, token-scoped permissions (e.g., function-calling disallowed for some tenants), model fallback circuitry, request-level ABAC checks (input tags).
   - Why: only runtime sees full context (cached KV, LLama cache state, ephemeral tokens) and can perform the most fine-grained checks.

5) Admin/control-plane APIs (management RBAC)
   - What to enforce: RBAC-heavy controls for role assignments, policy changes, audit-log access.
   - Why: separate admin plane with strict RBAC and MFA, distinct from runtime ABAC paths.

Policy semantics: hybrid model details
- RBAC layer: used for human and machine principals that perform management operations (create model, attach customer to dedicated pool, change policy). Roles map to capabilities and are checked on management endpoints.
- ABAC layer: evaluated per request and based on attributes: tenant_id, api_key_tier, route, model_tags (e.g., "no-export"), region, time_of_day, request_payload_flags.
- Combining rules: default deny; RBAC grants management-level actions; ABAC produces allow/deny/conditional (e.g., allow with scrub). Policies can return "advice" (e.g., require masking) not just boolean.

Policy precedence and overrides:
- Global central policies have baseline precedence. Regional policies can add constraints but cannot weaken global denies. Local (tenant) policies can be more restrictive but need to be recorded in Policy Catalog as effective overrides.
- Resolution algorithm (simple): evaluate denies first (global then regional then local), then evaluate allows. If conflict, highest precedence deny wins.

Performance and reliability considerations:
- Caching: policy bundles must be compact, signed, and cacheable at edge and routing services. Use Bloom filters or prefix trees for large allowlists.
- Latency budget: routing service should target <1ms additional latency for policy checks on cache hits. Cold-starts may use async prefetch during session warm-up.
- Graceful degradation: allow configurable fail-open/fail-closed per environment. Production: prefer fail-closed for management ops, fail-open for best-effort user routing (with alerts).
- Load: policy evaluation service should be horizontally scalable; heavy evaluations (regex, complex predicates) should be compiled to WASM or native expressions for speed.

Observability and auditing:
- Every decision must emit structured audit events: policy_id, evaluated_attributes (hashed where necessary), decision, enforcement_point, timestamp, bundle_version, request_id.
- Trace propagation: attach sampling span from edge to runtime; include decision latency.
- Regression alerts: when a policy change triggers >X% more denies or latency spikes, open an alert and auto-rollback hooks for emergency.

Security boundaries and trust model:
- The boundary between central control plane and regional data plane is a trust-limited control channel: bundles are signed, transport encrypted, and replay-protected.
- Admin channels require stricter authn (mTLS + MFA).
- For private/on-prem deployments, the customer-managed control plane pulls bundles; we require attestation proofs for bundle acceptance unless explicitly disabled.

Testing and rollout strategy:
- Stage 1 (greenfield): implement enforcement SDK with edge and routing insertion points in staging with synthetic workloads.
- Stage 2 (canary): push policy catalog updates to 1–2 low-traffic regions and enable blocking in audit-only mode first (decisions logged, not enforced).
- Stage 3 (enforce): enable enforcement with short TTL policies and monitor error spikes; rollback if critical.
- Test harness: policy fuzzing (random attribute combinations), unit tests for precedence, integration tests with Envoy plugin.

Operational playbook (short):
- Policy change flow: author -> review -> staging publish (audit-only) -> canary enforcement -> full rollout.
- Incident response: if a global policy causes outage, revert to last-known-good bundle and open an incident with root-cause on policy expression complexity.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How complex should central policy language be? Pros of expressiveness (fewer policies) vs cons (slower evaluation). Consider restricting language to boolean logic + numeric thresholds + limited regex.
- Should we support live-eval (central sync) for high-sensitivity policies (e.g., emergency kill-switch) vs bundle-based for speed? Hybrid approach suggested: emergency live channel for small set of policies.
- How do we represent temporal policies reliably (e.g., rate-limits over sliding windows) in a bundled, cacheable format?

Next steps / action items:
- A: Draft minimal policy schema (examples for deny-by-tenant, route-geo, model-variant-only) — owner: Priya — 2024-03-01
- B: Prototype enforcement SDK + Envoy filter example — owner: Mateo — 2024-03-15
- C: Build policy catalog UI wireframe in Console for non-engineers — owner: UX team (handoff) — 2024-04-01
- D: Run a staged canary with audit-only for us-west-2 region — owner: SRE — 2024-04-15

Appendix: quick policy examples (pseudocode)
1) Deny requests to dedicated pools from tenant X if origin != allowed-cidr:
  policy_id: deny-dedicated-tenantX-outside-cidr
  when: request.tenant == "tenant-X" && request.pool == "dedicated" && !(request.src_ip in tenantX_cidr)
  effect: deny

2) Conditional allow that requires PII-scrub:
  policy_id: allow-chatbot-embeds-if-scrubbed
  when: request.route == "/v1/chat" && request.model_tags contains "no-export"
  effect: allow with advice: require_masking=true

3) Admin RBAC check (management API):
  role: policy_admin
  permissions: [policy:create, policy:update, audit:read]
  evaluation: token.roles contains "policy_admin" && token.mfa == true

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally prescriptive: pick a small set of enforcement points and stick to them. Many past outages came from duplicated enforcement logic.
- We recommend keeping policy language compact and delegating heavy computations to compiled evaluation (WASM/native).
- Please add any missing enforcement points for private/on-prem topologies (I likely missed some edge cases).

Unresolved:
- Mapping of policy bundle TTL vs rollout velocity for high-frequency policy changes.
- Exact schema for representing temporal rules and sliding window counters in a bundle-friendly way.

End.
